newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr weathers c/a squall, buoyed by yen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr weathers c/a squall, buoyed by yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar survived a shock rise in the country's trade deficit with only superficial damage Wednesday as Japanese buyers remained undaunted.

The current account deficit widened 15 percent to A$1.69 billion in September when analysts had looked for another benign A$1.3 billion shortfall. A surprise fall in exports and upward revisions to the net income deficit were behind the worsening, which a few months ago would have hurt the dollar badly.
But now the currency was cushioned by its yield attraction to Japanese investors and, in any case, the market knew the data had few implications for its present obsession - interest rates.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar was keeping calm at US$0.7911/16 after easing as far as US$0.7905 after the data, and was little changed on Tuesday's late US$0.7910/15.

Traders reported good bids at 79 cents, partly linked to the issue of a dual currency samurai bond, but equally good offers at US$0.7925 where speculators were going short in anticipation of a domestic rate cut within the next week or two.

On the crosses it was whipped around by a very erratic US$/yen and at the close was modestly softer at 90.21/31 yen from 90.45.55 on Tuesday. In trade weighted terms it was unchanged from Tuesday's 58.7 finish.

Traders said flows out of Tokyo had been largely on the bid side but there were a couple of hasty selling bouts when a news agency reported a member of Japan's ruling LDP had called for a rise in interest rates there.
Dollar bulls have been counting on Japanese rates to remain at their record lows for months to come and so ensure the local currency maintains an attractive premium over the yen.

But analysts dismissed the rate comments as a sop for pensioners whose savings had been cut by the low rates, and seriously doubted the Bank of Japan would entertain a hike while the economic recovery there remained so fragile.
The bond market agreed and nudged the 10-year Japanese government bond yield down to a year low of 2.575 percent.

The yield on the Australian 10-year bond also headed lower to hit 7.40 percent from 7.52 on Tuesday, largely thanks to a soft set of wages data in the U.S. which were seen reducing the risk of a tightening by the Federal Reserve this year.
The same factor supported the local dollar as dealers ahd been worried the Fed would be raising rates while Australia was easing, thus narrowing the A$'s yield advantage all the more.
Most still expected the Reserve Bank to cut official rates by 0.5 point to 6.5 percent after its board meeting next week.
Today's current account figures came as a rude shock as the deficit had been trending comfortably lower this year, but were not expected to interfere with the timing of any easing.
Exports were the major culprit for the deterioration in the trade position with rural exports down seven percent in the month and non-rural exports off one percent.
That turned the balance on merchandise trade into a A$15 million deficit from a A$196 million surplus in August.
The fall in exports forced analysts to pare the contribution net exports would make to the expenditure measure of GDP in Q3, although it was still expected to be a healthy one.
Analyst estimates ranged from a 0.4 percent contribution right up to a full 1.0 point, a marked turnaround from the June quarter when exports detracted 0.9 point from GDP.

Data for September building approvals and retail sales on Thursday and Friday respectively would be slightly more relevant to the rate question, but again were not expected to budge the market from its easing expectations.

Approvals are forecast to be flat following gains of 1.6 percent and 8.1 percent in August and July respectively, while retail sales were seen easing 0.5 percent after a 1.0 percent rise in August. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
